Abstract
Recent advancements in Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI) aim to bridge the gap
between complex artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) models and human understanding, fostering
trust and usability in AI systems. However, challenges persist in comprehensively interpret-
ing these models, hindering their widespread adoption. This study addresses these challenges
by exploring recently emerging techniques in XAI. The primary problem addressed is the
lack of transparency and interpretability in AI models to humanity for institution-wide use,
which undermines user trust and inhibits their integration into critical decision-making pro-
cesses. Through an in-depth review, this study identiﬁes the objectives of enhancing the
interpretability of AI models and improving human understanding of their decision-making
processes.Variousmethodologicalapproaches,includingpost-hocexplanations,modeltrans-
parency methods, and interactive visualization techniques, are investigated to elucidate AI
model behaviours. We further present techniques and methods to make AI models more
interpretable and understandable to humans including their strengths and weaknesses to
demonstrate promising advancements in model interpretability, facilitating better compre-
hension of complex AI systems by humans. In addition, we provide the application of XAI
in local use cases. Challenges, solutions, and open research directions were highlighted to
clarify these compelling XAI utilization challenges. The implications of this research are
profound, as enhanced interpretability fosters trust in AI systems across diverse applications,
from healthcare to ﬁnance. By empowering users to understand and scrutinize AI decisions,
these techniques pave the way for more responsible and accountable AI deployment.

Progressively, various studies have attempted to address these peculiar challenges. For
instance, Lythe et al. [99] pinpointed that interpretability goes beyond explainability, aiming

and processes, enhancing visibility throughout the AI development and deployment stages.

such as feature attribution methods, rule-based models, and attention mechanisms that unveil
inﬂuential aspects of input data in model decisions. However, to our knowledge, none of

the deployment of AI. Ehsan et al. [39] qualitatively explain how an individual’s AI back-

intended design. These ﬁndings, which have signiﬁcant implications for XAI, reveal that
AI-generated explanations can inadvertently lead to negative consequences and potentially
harmful manipulation of trust. The authors propose design interventions to address these

2 Explanatory Depth of Explainable AI
In the context of XAI, explanatory depth refers to the extent of detail and clarity in the
explanations offered by AI systems. Some works have provided explanatory depth on XAI;
Chromik et al. [30] stated that explanatory depth shows how deeply an AI system can explain
its decisions, going beyond seeming or shallow explanations and the concept of explanatory
depth is vital because not all AI explanations are equally informative or useful. Some AI sys-
tems may provide high-level, imprecise explanations that do not help users understand the
underlying reasoning, while others can offer detailed, insightful explanations that enhance
user’s trust and comprehension [61]. So, Hulsen [65] in his work stated that XAI gives the
richness and detail of the explanations provided by AI systems in making AI more under-
standable and trustworthy, and achieving it involves various techniques and considerations to
ensure that the explanations are meaningful and helpful to users. There are various methods
used to achieve explanatory depth in XAI and these techniques include, Antoniadi et al. [8]
reviewed that feature importance that is the most inﬂuential feature in the decision-making
process is pointed out, Eberhard, [38] extracted that visualization using visual aids shows the
decision process and feature interactions, and Mittelstadt et al. [106] explained that counter-
factual explanations by showing what changes in input data would have resulted in a different
decision and local verse global explanations that offer insight into how a speciﬁc decision
was made (local) as well as how the overall model behaves (global). A recent study by Del
Ser et al. [34], introduced a framework for generating counterfactual explanations, formulat-
ing the task as a multi-objective optimization problem that balances three goals: plausibility,
change intensity, and adversarial effectiveness which uses generative adversarial networks
(GANs) to model input distribution, alongside a solver for multi-objective counterfactual
discovery, the framework addresses the envisaged peculiar problems. The study demon-
strates across six classiﬁcation tasks using image and 3D data conﬁrm evidence of trade-offs

2.2 Understandability of Artificial Intelligence Components
Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) is a diverse and multidisciplinary ﬁeld encompassing numerous
elements, methodologies, and specialized areas. These interconnected AI components often
collaborate within AI systems to tackle intricate challenges and execute tasks [70]. The
realm of AI research and development continually progresses, yielding novel techniques and
breakthroughs across its various domains. In studies by Arrieta et al. [10] and Montavon
et al. [108], "understandability" refers to both the extent to which a human can compre-
hend a model’s decision and the model’s capacity to elucidate its function to a human. AI
comprises several key components that synergize to empower machines to undertake tasks
typically requiring human intelligence. These AI components undertake diverse tasks, span-
ning from natural language comprehension and generation to image object recognition and
autonomous decision-making. By harnessing these capabilities, AI systems enhance human
intelligence, automate repetitive tasks, and tackle complex challenges across diverse ﬁelds.

present distinct challenges for explainability. Future research endeavors could concentrate on
devising innovative techniques that offer transparent explanations for deep learning models,
including attention mechanisms, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and recurrent neural
networks (RNNs) [66]. This may entail the exploration of approaches for visualizing and

gested that future research could focus on creating context-aware XAI techniques that adapt
explanations to the distinct characteristics of various local use cases, ensuring that AI systems
deliver interpretable and actionable insights that are meaningful and relevant to users.
(iv) Ethical and Social Implications: Future research in XAI should address the ethical
and social implications of explainable AI systems, particularly in local use cases where AI
applications can signiﬁcantly impact society. This includes tackling issues such as fairness,
transparency, accountability, and privacy in AI decision-making processes. Researchers could
investigate methods for detecting and mitigating biases in XAI systems to ensure explana-
tions are accurate, unbiased, and trustworthy. Additionally, it is important to examine the
broader societal implications of XAI, including its effects on job displacement, human-AI
collaboration, and the distribution of power and resources in society [139]. By considering
these ethical and social factors, researchers can ensure that XAI technologies are developed
and deployed responsibly, with careful consideration of their potential impacts on individuals,
communities, and society at large.

6 Conclusion
The recent advancements in Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI) represent a crucial
step toward bridging the gap between complex AI models and human understanding. By
improving explanatory depth, XAI techniques provide users with insights into AI decision-
making processes, thereby enhancing transparency and trust. As AI continues to evolve and
integrate into various societal sectors, the development of effective explanation methods
remains a priority in AI research and development. These explanations aim to make AI sys-
tem behavior transparent and interpretable to humans, fostering trust, accountability, and
informed decision-making across various applications. As demonstrated in this work, devel-
opers, operators, and users generally expect XAI to clarify key questions, enabling people to
fully understand and trust AI system decisions. This trust will allow users to have conﬁdence
in the models and encompass all XAI components related to transparency, causality, bias,
fairness, and safety. However, the lack of explainability and trust currently limits the full
utilization of AI systems.
Furthermore, the implementation of XAI in local use cases has great potential to improve
decision-making processes in various ﬁelds such as healthcare, ﬁnance, and law. However,
successful utilization requires careful consideration of local data characteristics, regulatory
requirements, and user preferences. As XAI continues to evolve, several key areas of future
research will shape its development. These include enhancing model transparency by devis-
ing methods to make complex AI models, like deep learning models, more transparent and
interpretable without signiﬁcantly compromising their performance. This research offers
practical implications, for instance, facilitating better decision-making processes in indus-
tries by providing transparent and interpretable insights into AI models. Also, implementing
emerging techniques in XAI can foster trust and acceptance among users, as they gain a deeper
understanding of AI model behaviour and reasoning, leading to increased conﬁdence in the
technology. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the importance of collaboration between
computer scientists, ethicists, psychologists, sociologists, and other disciplines, highlighting
the need for a holistic approach to address the multifaceted challenges of XAI effectively.

Abstract: Recent advancements in Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI) aim to bridge the gap between complex artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) models and human understanding, fostering trust and usability in AI systems. However, challenges persist in comprehensively interpret- ing these models, hindering their widespread adoption. This study addresses these challenges by exploring recently emerging techniques in XAI. The primary problem addressed is the lack of transparency and interpretability in AI models to humanity for institution-wide use, which undermines user trust and inhibits their integration into critical decision-making pro- cesses. Through an in-depth review, this study identiﬁes the objectives of enhancing the interpretability of AI models and improving human understanding of their decision-making processes.Variousmethodologicalapproaches,includingpost-hocexplanations,modeltrans- parency methods, and interactive visualization techniques, are investigated to elucidate AI model behaviours. We further present techniques and methods to make AI models more interpretable and understandable to humans including their strengths and weaknesses to demonstrate promising advancements in model interpretability, facilitating better compre- hension of complex AI systems by humans. In addition, we provide the application of XAI in local use cases. Challenges, solutions, and open research directions were highlighted to clarify these compelling XAI utilization challenges. The implications of this research are profound, as enhanced interpretability fosters trust in AI systems across diverse applications, from healthcare to ﬁnance. By empowering users to understand and scrutinize AI decisions, these techniques pave the way for more responsible and accountable AI deployment.
